title: Sarvam AI Launches Dictation API For English, 22 Indian Languages
summary: Sarvam AI launches dictation API supporting English and 22 Indian languages
detailed: Sarvam AI launched Sarvam Dictate, an API combining speech recognition and transcript editing, priced at ₹0.50 per minute of audio.
The API supports English and 22 Indian languages, utilizing the Saaras V4 speech recognition model paired with a dictation-trained Sarvam 105B LLM.
Sarvam claims the API required 40% fewer character edits for short English dictations and 47% fewer across Indian languages compared to Gemini 3.5 Transcribe.
This matters for developers building multilingual voice applications in a projected $1.8 billion Indian voice AI market by 2030.
sentences: Priced at ₹0.50 per minute of audio, the service combines speech recognition with transcript editing in a single API call.
It is designed to turn spoken inputs into text for messages, documents, and business records.
Dictate pairs the startup’s Saaras V4 speech recognition model with a version of its Sarvam 105B large language model trained for dictation.
The first transcribes the audio, while the second edits the resulting text.
Announcing the launch on X, Sarvam claimed that Dictate outperformed Google’s Gemini 3.5 Transcribe and AssemblyAI Dictation on a set of real-world dictation tests.
According to the startup, for English dictations of up to one minute, the API required 40% fewer character edits than Gemini 3.5 Transcribe.
Across Indian languages and Hinglish, the reduction stood at 47%.
For longer English dictations, Dictate required 11% fewer character edits than Gemini and 17% fewer than AssemblyAI.

Sarvam highlighted that its Dictate API is designed to account for the way people naturally speak, and can handle speakers switching between English and Indian languages mid-sentence, correcting themselves, and making false starts.
It also cleans up pauses and repetitions to produce a more refined transcript.

Developers can provide up to 1,000 names and technical terms per request, alongside contextual information such as customer relationship management (CRM) records, product lists, and a description of the situation.
They can also specify formatting preferences and choose how Indian languages and English appear in the output, including native scripts or Latin letters.
The API supports live dictation and uploaded recordings of up to an hour, returning both the raw transcript and edited text.
Its documented applications include chat messages, sales records, forms, and meeting minutes.
As per Sarvam, Dictate has already been tested through Kivi, its dictation application, where users have dictated more than 30 Mn words since launch.
The launch comes as AI developers increasingly integrate voice interfaces into applications for documentation, customer interactions, and data entry.
Potential uses span customer support, telehealth, medical documentation, and sales record updates, extending the scope for Sarvam’s multilingual voice AI offerings.
India’s linguistic diversity presents a significant opportunity for voice AI, with the domestic market projected to reach $1.8 Bn by 2030, according to Nasscom.
Startups are developing speech-to-text models to tap this demand for multilingual applications.

Earlier today, voice AI infrastructure startup Murf AI launched Finch, a streaming speech-to-text model that it claims ranks first across 11 Indian languages on the Voice of India benchmark, ahead of models from ElevenLabs, OpenAI, xAI, and Microsoft.
Murf claims Finch delivers a time-to-final-segment of 50 milliseconds and supports code-mixed speech and optional voice isolation.

Sarvam’s latest launch also follows the rollout of Token Factory, a platform that gives enterprises API access to its own models alongside global open-weight models, including Google’s Gemma and China’s DeepSeek.
Token Factory drew questions over whether Sarvam had used government-subsidised GPU capacity allocated for developing homegrown models to host foreign models.
The startup subsequently clarified that the platform runs on privately procured GPUs.
Reiterating its focus on model development, Sarvam said it will launch more models across vision, speech, and edge AI over the next two weeks.
